title: Researcher asks public to help track big, yellow spiders in Maryland
summary: An Eastern Shore biologist is asking for the public’s help reporting sightings in Maryland of a bright yellow invasive spider that looks scary but is actually harmless to humans.
content:
by Bay Journal, Maryland Matters December 10, 2025

by Bay Journal, Maryland Matters December 10, 2025

By Jeremy Cox
The Chesapeake Bay Journal

An Eastern Shore biologist is asking for the public’s help reporting sightings in Maryland of a bright yellow invasive spider that looks scary but is actually harmless to humans.

Washington College professor Angela Chuang says the Joro spider, Trichonephila clavata, is easiest to spot in the late fall when the adult females reach their maximum size, with a leg span of up to 4 inches. She is calling for observers to snap photographs of the spiders and report them in the iNaturalist app.

Chuang said it isn’t uncommon to spot the species in large numbers in Georgia, Tennessee and other parts of the South. They weren’t documented in Maryland until 2022, when they were found  in Elkridge.

“The main thing is, we would like it if people could report when they see these spiders, so we have a better understanding of how Joro spiders are spreading around, especially because this is a distinct population from the older one,” Chuang said. “It represents an opportunity to study an invasive population at its earliest stages.”

The Joro spiders’ yellow bodies and black legs make it easy to mistake them for yellow garden spiders, which are Maryland natives. The Asian Joros don’t seem to pose a danger to humans or pets, and tests have shown their bites to cause little or no reaction in subjects.

Still, Chuang is concerned about the impact they might have on local wildlife, particularly local spider communities. When they settle into a new region, Joro spiders tend to quickly become the dominant species, she said. People in the Baltimore and Eastern Shore areas should be especially on the lookout, she added.

Residents of those areas can email the researcher directly at JoroSpidersWC@gmail.com to invite her team to their properties to study them.
